Marrick
MAR-ik
n. (the Benedictine nunnery in Swaledale, founded c. 1154, dissolved 1540)
Old Norse marr and rik or Old English ric, a boundary strip by the fen; Domesday forms include Marige.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Marrick Priory was founded about 1154 in Swaledale by Roger de Aske for Benedictine nuns, and it remained a small and poor community of between twelve and sixteen women for nearly four centuries. Its records are unusually ordinary: rents, a mill, a few sheep pastures, lead-mining dues in the dale, and the lists of names at each election of a prioress. It was dissolved in 1540, when the last prioress and sixteen nuns were pensioned. The church tower stands, and the buildings became a farm and later a residential centre. The dictionary records Marrick because the female houses are routinely left out of the account, and because what they offered a woman in medieval England was real: literacy, a settled community, and an alternative to marriage or service. Scripture honours the unmarried state as a calling and not as a higher order — and the Reformers' quarrel was with the vow, not the women. “Forbidding to marry, and commanding to abstain from meats, which God hath created to be received with thanksgiving” (1Ti 4:3) names the error precisely, and it is an error about God's creation rather than about anyone's sincerity.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines a nunnery as a house for nuns; a prioress as the female superior of a priory; a pension as an allowance for past service; celibacy as the unmarried state; and thanksgiving as the act of rendering thanks.

expand to see more

NUNNERY, n. A house in which nuns reside; a cloister or retired place in which females live sequestered from the world.

PRIORESS, n. A female superior of a convent of nuns.

PENSION, n. An annual allowance of a sum of money to a person by government, or to an individual, for past services.

CELIBACY, n. An unmarried state; a single life; most frequently applied to the voluntary single life of a priest.

THANKSGIVING, n. The act of rendering thanks or expressing gratitude for favors or mercies.

Key Scripture

1Ti 4:3 — "Forbidding to marry, and commanding to abstain from meats, which God hath created to be received with thanksgiving of them which believe and know the truth."

1Ti 4:1 — "Now the Spirit speaketh expressly, that in the latter times some shall depart from the faith, giving heed to seducing spirits, and doctrines of devils;"

Jam 1:27 — "Pure religion and undefiled before God and the Father is this, To visit the fatherless and widows in their affliction, and to keep himself unspotted from the world."

Psa 100:4 — "Enter into his gates with thanksgiving, and into his courts with praise: be thankful unto him, and bless his name."

Modern Corruption

Small Benedictine nunnery in Swaledale, founded c. 1154, dissolved 1540 with a prioress and sixteen nuns pensioned.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the quarrel was with the vow and not with the women. Paul names the thing itself, “Forbidding to marry, and commanding to abstain from meats, which God hath created to be received with thanksgiving” (1Ti 4:3), and the sentence is about creation: meat and marriage are God's and are to be received. He places it in a list of predicted departures, “in the latter times some shall depart from the faith, giving heed to seducing spirits, and doctrines of devils” (1Ti 4:1), which is a strong word and his own.

The live temptation, from either direction, is to turn Marrick's sixteen women into an argument. They were not an argument; they were a community that gave poor gentlewomen in a hard dale a literate and settled life. James' measure of religion fits them as well as anyone, “To visit the fatherless and widows in their affliction, and to keep himself unspotted from the world” (Jam 1:27), and the gratitude Paul insists on over marriage and meat is the same gratitude the Psalter asks at the gate, “Enter into his gates with thanksgiving, and into his courts with praise” (Psa 100:4).

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek koluo (G2967), to forbid; Greek aphistemi (G0868), to depart from; Greek eucharistia (G2169), thanksgiving; Greek ktizo (G2936), to create.

expand to see more

Greek koluo (G2967) — to hinder, to forbid; “Forbidding to marry, and commanding to abstain from meats, which God hath created to be received with thanksgiving”, 1 Timothy 4:3.

Greek eucharistia (G2169) — thanksgiving, gratitude; “Forbidding to marry, and commanding to abstain from meats, which God hath created to be received with thanksgiving”, 1 Timothy 4:3.

Greek aphistemi (G0868) — to withdraw from, to depart; “in the latter times some shall depart from the faith, giving heed to seducing spirits, and doctrines of devils”, 1 Timothy 4:1.

Greek threskeia (G2356) — religion, outward worship; “To visit the fatherless and widows in their affliction, and to keep himself unspotted from the world”, James 1:27.

Hebrew todah (H8426) — thanksgiving, praise; “Enter into his gates with thanksgiving, and into his courts with praise”, Psalm 100:4.

Usage

"“Forbidding to marry, and commanding to abstain from meats, which God hath created to be received with thanksgiving” (1Ti 4:3) — the error named precisely."

"“in the latter times some shall depart from the faith, giving heed to seducing spirits, and doctrines of devils” (1Ti 4:1) — Paul's own word for it."

"“To visit the fatherless and widows in their affliction, and to keep himself unspotted from the world” (Jam 1:27) — the measure that fits Marrick's women too."
